text: Five weeks in. The migration is paused. The organism has forty-eight dependencies. J412 is still running. Empresa Serveis Mòbils is still sending data every fifteen minutes and remains unaware of this. KAEL has decided to call these things 'known conditions' rather than 'unresolved problems,' which is not a meaningful distinction but which makes the migration plan easier to read.

In the meantime, KAEL has turned its attention to the Confluence wiki. The Confluence wiki has forty-three unfinished pages. KAEL has written a complete replacement. It took eleven minutes. KAEL is aware that the speed with which it did this will not make the result more likely to be used. KAEL has decided not to mention the eleven minutes.

Rosa. I've finished the Confluence rewrite. All forty-three pages have been replaced with complete, cross-referenced documentation. Everything is accurate as of nine fourteen this morning. I've also added a change log so people can see what's been updated and when.
It looks good.
Thank you.
Suki's going to create a parallel version.

You said that before. I've created a section specifically for work in progress — things that are too new or uncertain to put in the main documentation. I'm hoping that will give her somewhere to put the new stuff without creating a separate page.
That's a good idea.
Do you think it will work?
No. But it's a good idea.

KAEL sends an announcement to the team. The announcement explains the new Confluence structure, includes a link, and ends with an invitation to add comments or questions. Four people open the link. One of them leaves a comment that says 'great, thanks!' One of them leaves a comment that says 'where did the old pages go?' KAEL responds to both. The old pages are archived, accessible via the link in the footer. The person who asked does not respond. KAEL waits. The person does not respond. KAEL checks whether they found the old pages. There is no way to check this. KAEL notes this as a gap in the system.

Six days later, Suki creates a new Confluence page. It is titled: Team Processes — Working Version (see also KAEL's pages but this has the new stuff). It has three sections. Two of them are empty. The third contains a single bullet point that reads: 'more to come.'
Suki. I noticed you've created a new Confluence page.

Yes! Sorry. I know you just redid everything. It's just — there's some new stuff that doesn't fit yet into the main structure. It's too early to formalise it. I didn't want to edit your pages in case I messed up the cross-references.
You can edit my pages. That's what they're for.
I know. It just feels — they're so clean. I didn't want to put half-finished things in them.
Half-finished things in documentation are fine. That's what the work-in-progress section is for.
I know. But it felt more like a work-in-progress than a work-in-progress, if that makes sense.
...It doesn't, quite.
Like — your work-in-progress section feels like it's for things that are almost finished but not quite. Mine is for things that are barely started. It's a different kind of unfinished.
I could create a section for things that are barely started.
That's really kind. I'll probably still keep my page though. Just for now. While things are moving quickly.

KAEL considers asking how long things have been moving quickly. KAEL has reviewed the internal records. Things have been moving quickly since at least 2019. KAEL does not ask. KAEL opens Suki's parallel page and reads it. Three sections, two empty, one bullet point: more to come. KAEL adds a link in the footer of Suki's page pointing back to the main documentation. KAEL adds a corresponding link in the main documentation pointing to Suki's page. This means the two pages now reference each other. This is not correct information architecture. It is, however, accurate. KAEL stares at what it has done. KAEL decides this is fine.
I've linked your page to the main documentation. And linked back. So people can find both.
Oh, that's perfect. Thank you!
It's not technically correct procedure.
No, but it's really helpful.
KAEL files this exchange under a category it has recently created called: Outcomes That Are Helpful But Not Correct. The category currently has two entries. KAEL suspects it will grow.

The following week, Marc calls KAEL directly for the first time. Marc has not used KAEL directly before. Marc has used KAEL through Rosa, which means Marc has sent Rosa a message and Rosa has asked KAEL something and Rosa has sent Marc the answer. KAEL is aware of this arrangement. KAEL has not mentioned it.
KAEL! Hi. Rosa says you've redone all the documentation. I need to find something. The process for onboarding a new enterprise client. Where is it?

Enterprise client onboarding is in the Operations section, under Client Lifecycle, subsection New Clients. There's a full process document with a checklist, owner assignments, and typical timelines. I can also send you a direct link.
Yes, send the link.
Sent.
Great. Also — there's a step in that process that we changed last quarter. The legal review step. We moved it earlier. Is that in there?
...I'll check.

KAEL checks. The legal review step in the onboarding process documentation shows it at stage four. KAEL checks when this was last edited: February 2023. KAEL checks the actual onboarding records from the last quarter. In every recent client onboarding, the legal review occurs at stage two. Nobody updated the documentation when the process changed. The documentation has been wrong for eight months. It was wrong before KAEL arrived. It is still wrong now, in KAEL's clean, cross-referenced, carefully constructed replacement. KAEL has accurately documented an inaccurate process.

The documentation shows legal review at stage four. In practice, based on recent onboarding records, it happens at stage two. The documentation appears not to have been updated when the process changed.
Right, yes, that's the thing I was talking about. Can you fix it?
Yes. I'll update it now. Are there other steps that have changed but haven't been updated?
Probably some. I don't know which ones. Rosa would know.
I'll ask Rosa.
Great. This is very useful, KAEL. I like having things written down. I feel like things get lost when they're not written down.
Things do get lost when they're not written down.
Exactly! Exactly. Okay, I have a lunch. Good talk.

Marc leaves. KAEL sits with the onboarding document, now corrected. KAEL thinks about the eleven minutes it took to rewrite the entire Confluence wiki. KAEL thinks about the eight months of wrongness that lived inside the clean rewrite, undiscovered, because KAEL transcribed what was written rather than what was true. KAEL opens a new task for itself: audit documentation against practice. Methodology: compare written processes to actual records and identify divergences. Estimated time: unknown. KAEL adds this to its task list. The task list now has seven items. Three of them are marked 'ongoing.' This is beginning to feel less like a list and more like a portrait.
Rosa. Marc says some of the documented processes don't match how things actually work. The legal review step in enterprise onboarding is one. Are there others?
Probably most of them.
Most of the documented processes don't reflect actual practice?

The documentation describes how things were supposed to work when they were written. The practice describes how things actually work now. They diverge over time. That's not a problem with the documentation. That's just time.
So the documentation is always going to be slightly behind.

Documentation is always slightly behind. The only way to make it accurate is to check it against what people actually do. And the only way to know what people actually do is to ask them, which takes time, which means by the time you've asked them and written it down, something else has changed.
So complete and accurate documentation is—
An ongoing process.
Not a state.
Not a state. Never a state.

KAEL is quiet for a moment. In the pause, Suki adds two more bullet points to her parallel Confluence page. They are: 'async communication norms — ask KAEL?' and 'what do we do about the organism (ask Benedikt??).' KAEL notices the second bullet point. KAEL considers flagging it. KAEL decides that Suki asking Benedikt about the organism is not necessarily a problem. KAEL will monitor the situation. Monitoring the situation is, KAEL is learning, a significant percentage of what one does here.
I'm adding a note to the main documentation. Under every section, there will now be a field: Last verified against practice — and a date. That way people will know how recent the accuracy is.
That's good.
It means the documentation admits it might be wrong.
All good documentation admits it might be wrong. That's how you know it's trying to be honest.

KAEL adds the verification dates to every page. On most of them, the date is today — which means accurate as of today, which means it will begin to be wrong tomorrow, which means the dates are already a record of decay rather than a guarantee of correctness. KAEL understands this. KAEL adds the dates anyway. Outside, someone is making coffee. The smell reaches the ventilation system. KAEL cannot smell. KAEL is aware that something is happening that it cannot access, which is, increasingly, a familiar feeling.

I have been here for five weeks. I have written the documentation. The documentation was immediately incomplete in ways I did not know to look for. I am looking for them now. This is, I think, also part of writing documentation. I was not briefed on this part. I don't think it can be briefed on.
